articles.title: Messi reina entre las camisetas más vendidas de la MLS por cuarta temporada consecutiva
articles.standfirst: El futbolista del Inter Miami lidera el ranking de las camisetas más populares de la competición
articles.summary: El futbolista del Inter Miami lidera el ranking de las camisetas más populares de la competición
articles.body: Leo Messi sigue reinando en la MLS. Lo hace en el campo, y también en las tiendas. Su camiseta es la más vendida entre las 30 franquicias de la competición por cuarta temporada consecutiva, según ha informado la propia liga. La MLS no ha dado datos sobre el número de camisetas Adidas –su socio técnico exclusivo– del 10 del Inter Miami que se han comercializado, pero sí ha ofrecido un ranking con los diez jugadores que más rendimientos dan en el negocio del retail de los equipos. Destaca la presencia de grandes futbolistas que han pasado por LaLiga recientemente. Además del delantero argentino, también aparecen Robert Lewandowski (4º), que ha fichado este verano por el Chicago Fire; Antoine Griezmann (5º), nueva estrella del Orlando City SC; y dos compañeros de Messi en Miami: Luis Suárez (8º) y Rodrigo de Paul (10º). En el podio, Messi está acompañado por dos futbolistas que también llegaron a la MLS en los últimos años procedente de un gran club europeo: Heung-min Son (2º) y Thomas Müller (3º). El top-10 lo completan el nuevo talento estadounidense Cavan Sullivan (6º), el gabonés Denis Bouanga (7º) y el alemán Hany Mukhtar (9º).

articles.title: 49ers injury updates: Christian Kirk doesn’t practice on Thursday
articles.summary: Christian Kirk missed Thursday’s session after being a limited participant on Wednesday
articles.body:
The San Francisco 49ers injury report is out for Thursday. As usual, Trent Williams returned to practice after a veteran's day off.

Christian McCaffrey participated on a limited basis. McCaffrey didn't practice Wednesday, but it wasn't because of a rest day, so it's good to see McCaffrey return to practice after dealing with a hamstring injury.

The only other change from Wednesday was Christian Kirk. The wide receiver was listed as "Did not participate" with a knee injury after being limited on Wednesday.

General manager John Lynch already said the team would be without wideouts Deebo Samuel (hamstring) and Mike Evans (ribs/Achilles) this Sunday.

So, the 49ers would essentially be swapping Demarcus Robinson, who was again limited with an ankle injury, for Kirk if he cannot play.

There's the "what if" Brandon Aiyuk suits up with the wide receiver depth depleted, but he hasn't practiced or played with the team in over a calendar year. Aiyuk may have played his fair share of pickup games on the basketball court, but that doesn't come close to simulating what an NFL game is like.

And that's before you get into, you know, the other Aiyuk stuff.

articles.title: Steelers Insider Shares Verdict on Potential WR Trade
articles.summary: The Pittsburgh Steelers are in an ideal spot at the moment. The team is 6-2 and in the midst of a bye week, sitting in first place in the AFC North.The bye m...
articles.body:
The Pittsburgh Steelers are in an ideal spot at the moment. The team is 6-2 and in the midst of a bye week, sitting in first place in the AFC North.

The bye means the team won't play another game before the November 10 trade deadline. This gives fans plenty of time to come up with potential trades to pitch and discuss.

One area of particular focus is at the wide receiver position. DK Metcalf has been a massive disappointment this season, though he does still lead the team with 378 receiving yards. Yet the next closest actual wide receiver to him on the leaderboard is Germie Bernard with 284 yards.

Aaron Rodgers has relied upon Jaylen Warren, Darnell Washington, and Pat Freiermuth to help pick up the slack. However, the 6-2 start could mean the Steelers want to make a splash and pair Rodgers with a top talent in his final NFL season.

One longtime Steelers insider shut down any optimism of such an addition .

Steelers Insider Shuts Down Potential WR Trade

Gerry Dulac covers the Steelers for the Pittsburgh Post-Gazette and recently took on a series of questions during the bye week.

He was directly asked about the chances of the Steelers trading for a receiver in exchange for draft capital. His response?

"They are not doing that," he wrote . "They already did that when they traded for Pittman."

Dulac is of course referring to Michael Pittman Jr., who has only appeared in three games thus far for the Steelers. He has seven receptions for 89 yards and is currently out on injured reserve.

The Steelers traded for Pittman back in March and expected him to be a top contributor alongside Metcalf. That can still happen once he returns, but the early returns are not promising.

The Steelers could always find the perfect deal and prove Dulac wrong. However, the longtime reporter's statement does seem to indicate the 6-2 Steelers have faith that players like Metcalf, Pittman, and even Roman Wilson will step up during the second half of the season.

Both Pittman and Wilson are on IR, so their individual returns can be viewed as a type of late-season acquisition.

Bernard has shown flashes as of late and it appears the true strength of this offense lies with Warren and the running game.

Steelers fans are understandably impatient given the team hasn't won a playoff game since the 2016 season. The front office may simply decide the impending return of someone like Pittman is a better option than a trade at this point in time.

articles.title: Clemson freshman QB pokes fun at Florida State’s empty stadium before Syracuse game
articles.summary: Noise in the Clemson Tigers’ media center forced quarterback Tait Reynolds to wait during his press conference on Wednesday, Nick Kosko noted for On3, and th...
articles.body:
Noise in the Clemson Tigers' media center forced quarterback Tait Reynolds to wait during his press conference on Wednesday, Nick Kosko noted for On3, and the interruption sent the freshman's mind back to Saturday's trip to Tallahassee.

"I think Florida State was playing some crowd noise. It got louder throughout the game. There was nobody there. It got loud. I was like, 'What the heck?'" Reynolds said with a smile.

Reynolds was joking, and the joke landed because of how the last week has gone for the Florida State Seminoles.

Before Clemson's 36-24 win on Oct. 31, a plane circled Doak Campbell Stadium towing a banner that called for the firing of head coach Mike Norvell and the removal of board chairman Peter Collins, with Norvell's name misspelled. Dabo Swinney brought it up afterward, on behalf of the opposing coach.

"It was embarrassing what I saw above the stadium. Whoever did that, man, you ought to be ashamed of yourself. And they didn't even spell his name right," Swinney said.

Florida State played the fourth quarter in front of a mostly empty stadium and fired Norvell the next day, ending a seven-year run at 41-39. Rick Stockstill is now the interim coach of a 3-5 team.

Why did Doak Campbell Stadium get loud with so few fans left?

A less scandalous explanation than a sound system sits in the box score: Florida State trailed 29-10 with under nine minutes to play, then scored 14 straight points to make it 29-24. Whoever had stayed finally had something to yell about. Reynolds ended it on third-and-12 with 3:17 left, running 79 yards for a touchdown, the longest run ever by a Clemson quarterback.

Clemson entered the game with two touchdown passes all season, the fewest in FBS, and had gone four games without one, its longest drought since 2005. Reynolds threw two against Florida State, finishing 18 of 32 for 189 yards, and added 85 rushing yards on 14 carries. That was quite a night for a quarterback who in September became the earliest freshman to start for Clemson in more than 50 years , and it helps explain the mood on Wednesday.

The win moved Clemson to 5-3 and 3-2 in the ACC, one victory from bowl eligibility. The next stop is the indoor JMA Wireless Dome, where the Tigers face the Syracuse Orange at noon ET on Saturday on ESPN2.

articles.title: Ravens place QBs Lamar Jackson, Tyler Huntley on injured reserve
articles.summary: The Baltimore Ravens placed quarterbacks Lamar Jackson and Tyler Huntley on injured reserve on Thursday ahead of their Week 9 matchup with the Jacksonville J...
articles.body:
The Baltimore Ravens placed quarterbacks Lamar Jackson and Tyler Huntley on injured reserve on Thursday ahead of their Week 9 matchup with the Jacksonville Jaguars.

Jackson is set to undergo thumb surgery with discouraging reports but no firm timeline from the team regarding his potential return later this year. Huntley's turf toe is thought to be season-ending, though again, the Ravens have yet to confirm. Both will miss a minimum of four games after landing on IR, making them eligible to return after Baltimore's Week 13 bye.

Undrafted rookie Joe Fagnano will start against Jacksonville on Thursday night. Once the Ravens finalize acquiring Jacoby Brissett from the Cardinals, he will likely take over in Week 10 against the Los Angeles Chargers.

The Ravens will drop to 4-5 with a likely loss to the Jaguars. The winless Chargers are about as beatable as they come, and the Texans and Panthers are a combined 5-9. Getting to 6-7 before the bye seems possible, but making the postseason after that relies on a successful return from Jackson. The two-time MVP has stated his reluctance to play before he is healthy enough to do so already this year; feeling comfortable with an injured throwing hand might be an even higher bar to clear.

The Ravens promoted Austin Reed from the practice squad to the active roster to back up Fagnano on Thursday night. Kedon Slovis will serve as the emergency No. 3 quarterback.

Baltimore also elevated outside linebacker Adisa Isaac and kicker Jake Moody from the practice squad to face the Jaguars. Isaac adds depth off the edge and on special teams after Tavius Robinson's season-ending injury, while Moody replaces Tyler Loop after his IR placement on Tuesday.

articles.title: Back surgery will keep Robert Kraft from Rob Gronkowski's Patriots Hall of Fame induction
articles.summary: Patriots owner Robert Kraft recently underwent back surgery, which will keep him sidelined on "injured reserve" and force him to miss Rob Gronkowski's induct...
articles.body:
Patriots owner Robert Kraft recently underwent back surgery, which will keep him sidelined on "injured reserve" and force him to miss Rob Gronkowski's induction into the Patriots Hall of Fame on Saturday.

"As much pain as I was in before having surgery, it pains me even more to miss the ceremony," Kraft, 85, told Mike Reiss of ESPN on Thursday.

Doctors ordered Kraft to stay off his feet, so he will also miss the Patriots' game against the Packers on Sunday and the trip to Munich for a Week 10 game against the Lions.

Fans voted Gronkowski into the Patriots Hall of Fame in April in his first year of eligibility.

Gronkowski, having undergone multiple back surgeries during his playing career, understood Kraft's absence, the owner said.

"I always told Gronk that in my next life, I wanted to come back as him, because I had never seen him have a bad day. But after a couple of back surgeries, I take that back. I never want to experience that again," Kraft said.

articles.title: Cleveland Browns are still struggling to change the team’s culture
articles.summary: Two plays from the loss in Pittsburgh highlight how far the team still has to go to stop being bullied.
articles.body:
The Cleveland Browns have long been the league's little brother that other teams like to bully, especially in the AFC North.

There have been times over the years when a player has tried to insert that missing level of fight back, with former quarterback Baker Mayfield coming to mind.

Even though Mayfield is five years and three teams removed from the Browns, he has not lost any of his feistiness, which was on full display during Sunday's game against the Atlanta Falcons.

While attempting to block down the field on Kenny Gainwell's fourth-quarter touchdown run, Mayfield was dumped into a mud puddle by Atlanta safety Jessie Bates III. Mayfield popped back up, but more importantly, one of his offensive linemen quickly came to his defense and got after Bates.

Now contrast that with two plays from Sunday as the Browns were once again bullied by the Steelers.

On the game's opening possession, quarterback Deshaun Watson took a helmet-to-helmet hit from Pittsburgh safety Jaquan Brisker that left Watson lying face down on the field. While he was able to return to the game, Watson suffered a concussion that will likely sideline him for this week's game against the New Orleans Saints.

Later in the game, defensive end Jared Verse was dangerously dropped on his head by Pittsburgh offensive lineman Mason McCormick during an extra-point attempt. Verse was fortunate that he was not injured in what was clearly a dirty play.

Brisker and McCormick were both penalized for the plays, but did anyone on the Browns stick up for Watson or Verse? Did a lineman let Brisker know that the quarterback is off limits? Or call out McCormick?

If you have watched the Browns for any time, you know the answer to those questions.

Watson has not commented on the hit as he is busy recovering in the league-mandated concussion protocol. But on Thursday, Verse let it be known that he was not happy that no one stepped up when he went down, according to Mary Kay Cabot at cleveland.com :

"The lack of reaction by those around me upset me a lot. Not any aspect of anybody; we're focused on the game and everything like that. But a similar play happened to Derek Barnett; I think the next field goal and I spazzed. I lost it because it was my brother and my teammate. When you do something like that, it really upsets me very deeply. "So, I could tell that from that point on, I was like, we have to do better. We have to get better on every aspect of the game of being mentally aware of, these are my brothers and we're not fighting for each other. We're just kind of focused on the one aspect of the game."

"The lack of reaction by those around me upset me a lot. Not any aspect of anybody; we're focused on the game and everything like that. But a similar play happened to Derek Barnett; I think the next field goal and I spazzed. I lost it because it was my brother and my teammate. When you do something like that, it really upsets me very deeply.

"So, I could tell that from that point on, I was like, we have to do better. We have to get better on every aspect of the game of being mentally aware of, these are my brothers and we're not fighting for each other. We're just kind of focused on the one aspect of the game."

Several of Verse's teammates, including linebackers Carson Schwesinger and Quincy Williams, said they did not see the play, while Barnett said he would have defended Verse if he had seen the play, but cautioned that the Browns can't let a situation like that get out of hand.

No one is looking for the Browns to turn into the Oakland Raiders of the 1970s, although they were the only team that stood up to the Steelers, so maybe a little bit of that attitude would be nice.

Winning, of course, is the best revenge. But if the Browns are truly committed to changing the culture of the team, which is something that Verse has been vocal about since arriving in town from the Los Angeles Rams, then standing up for a fallen teammate from time to time would not be such a bad idea.

articles.title: LIV Golf roiled the game for years. What will its legacy be now?
articles.summary: LIV Golf is no more, bringing to an end a wild, eventful and odd chapter of professional golf.
articles.body:
Five years and one week ago, a press release hit the web at 8 a.m. It announced, for the first time, a new, Saudi-backed golf company helmed by Greg Norman named LIV Golf Investments. It was, of course, the parent of LIV Golf, a rival league designed to completely alter the professional side of the sport. And it did. But now, more than half a decade later, that company will soon cease to exist as LIV will "not proceed with a LIV 2.0 plan," according to its lawyers in bankruptcy court Thursday morning, and will move to wind down its business.

The beginning of this end came seven months ago, when the Saudi Public Investment Fund — after injecting more than $5 billion into the outfit — elected to suddenly cease funding the league, just weeks after one of its most successful events in South Africa . The world had changed since 2021, and even since 2025, particularly in the Middle East, where Saudi Arabia and its neighbors were pulled into geopolitical conflict. The PIF had decided LIV was "no longer consistent" with its strategy, and a report from the Financial Times confirmed it, calling into question if the league would even be able to finish its 2026 season. After all, it was funded entirely by repeated installments from the PIF, signed for by its governor, Yasir Al-Rumayyan, which often cleared $300 million.

What wasn't clear then has become clear in recent months — that the decision did not involve any LIV management at all. It came from the top of the PIF, which officially added two investment bankers who specialize in bankruptcy restructuring — Gene Davis and Jon Zinman — on April 13, one day after the 2026 Masters and two days before reports of the league's demise. Though it set off a harried week in Mexico City, where LIV was playing that week, with reports of players not receiving expected payments, the PIF decided to fund the league for the rest of its season. But quietly, the finances of the league did not add up.

In June, during the U.S. Open, the PIF materially changed its financial relationship with the league, loaning LIV money rather than injecting it with funds for greater equity. From June through its initial bankruptcy filing, that secured loan tallied to $495 million, much of which was paid to players and league employees, like CEO Scott O'Neil, who received a retention payment of $6.375 million in late June. On the short side of that draw were dozens of vendors that had been doing business with the league for months and were not paid. The spectrum of companies varied widely, from numerous broadcast technology brands to the State of Louisiana, to Uber and Equinox, all the way down to a Georgia catering company — a reminder of just how extravagant the league's spending had become. LIV's unpaid bills eventually came to the fore in August in the form of lawsuits, which O'Neil was asked about, point-blank, during LIV's final event in Indianapolis. He balked at clarifying any resolution and at the reality of bankruptcy, but just days later O'Neil and LIV began the formal process of stripping team ownership from the stars it had once wooed into its ranks.

The last eight weeks of bankruptcy court have forced LIV to share its warts in public, adding context to statements the league might have previously gloated about. The league was hosting $30 million events but making next to no money from its broadcast rights — the golden goose for sports leagues around the world. In August, it earned a $300 million investment proposal from London-based BC Partners Credit, which the league was quick to revel in but what amounted to exit financing from what the league owed to the PIF. Documents revealed it to be a last-ditch deal that gave BC Partners near-total control. In the event that enough players agreed to stick with the league, BC Partners would take a minority (though significant) ownership stake and benefit from LIV's billions in net operating losses, a sizable tax asset. But it had to land enough commitments from players — particularly its biggest stars — to earn BC Partners' approval. A big part of that came down to Jon Rahm, the league's sure-fire best player, whose contract was worth 40 times that of lesser LIV players. Rahm was coy about his interest in the league's future all summer, right until an October court hearing, where his representation announced he was not accepting the terms of LIV 2.0. Rahm's lack of interest proved to be a domino, setting off a number of departures from the league's biggest names: Sergio Garcia, Ian Poulter, Louis Oosthuizen, Tyrrell Hatton.

That all led to a Wednesday report from the Financial Times that LIV had not landed enough commitments to convince BC Partners to finalize its financing. On Thursday morning, the announcement lasted about 10 minutes and was succeeded by a statement from a BC Partners spokesperson:

"While there was great support for the league, we are disappointed that mutually acceptable terms could not be reached among the various stakeholders. We commend LIV Golf's management for their tireless efforts and thank the players who supported the future of LIV and engaged constructively throughout. We wish them every success as they continue their careers."

In a matter of minutes, LIV issued perhaps its final press release, saying, "The league is proud of the role it has played in shaping the broader golf landscape, from introducing team golf at the professional level to bringing world-class events to new markets, and it believes its impact on the sport will be felt for years to come."

That is undoubtedly true. The ubiquitousness of $20 million purses (or higher), the prevalence of team golf and increased importance of the major championships are all results of LIV Golf's five-year journey. But the league's funnels of money being turned off by its ultra-wealthy backer is fitting, if not ironic. Its existence has always been entirely about money — how much of it the Saudi PIF wanted to provide, and how much top-end pro golfers wanted to chase.

THE END OF LIV GOLF WAS, IN WAYS, LIKE ITS BEGINNING. Its infancy was ominous, back in February 2022, when its leading man, Greg Norman, boastfully railed against then PGA Tour commissioner, Jay Monahan. Norman had inked a number of players to non-disclosure agreements, but the league couldn't fully come forward with its plans for fear of Tour retribution. That spring, it was just waiting for months to pass before it could officially launch. But Phil Mickelson quotes published that month called into question the purpose of the league and its Saudi Arabian backing. Numerous players flipped — at least publicly — pledging their allegiance to the PGA Tour while Mickelson eventually took a leave of absence — losing longtime sponsors in the process — shrouding the forthcoming league in mystery. Even LIV staff was unsure how the league would proceed.

But it was during those immediate weeks after Mickelson's quotes were published that Al-Rumayyan seemed to double down, and with pace. Before long, the operative was to not only launch in 2022, but to get it done in a three-month timeframe. It signed 17 of the top 100 golfers in the world, held a swanky draft party on the outskirts of London and produced a very loud tournament that kicked off on June 9, 2022. Music blared through speakers all over the property, a jarring change for golf traditionalists, but the most emphatic news was delivered in print: a letter from Monahan promising that the 17 players who held some sort of PGA Tour membership were suspended . Ten of them had already resigned, making it clear — if it wasn't already — that this was a golf war.

LIV moved forward bold and nimble — even getting Al-Rumayyan to pledge a $54 million prize to any player who might card a perfect score of 54 in a round — while the PGA Tour held tightly to its membership regulations, which players sign every year. The Tour faced the ominous, near-constant threat of more players defecting — Brooks Koepka, Bryson DeChambeau, Patrick Reed and Cam Smith would join LIV in the coming weeks — while LIV faced something more political. Victims of 9/11 families protested at some of its events — accusing the players and the league of sportswashing Saudi Arabia's human rights record. Monahan even invoked that tragedy in a broadcast interview on national TV alongside Jim Nantz: "I would ask that any player that has left, or that would ever consider leaving, have you ever had to apologize for being a member of the PGA Tour?"

Within months, LIV players and the league filed a lawsuit against the Tour for anti-competitive practices and restraint of trade. The Tour filed a countersuit in return, and the legal process inched ever so expensively toward deposition of Al-Rumayyan. Legal costs mounted for the Tour, tallying near $50 million, according to a source with familiarity of the proceedings. And so, in April 2023, Jimmy Dunne, then an independent director for the Tour's policy board, reached out to a representative of Al-Rumayyan to coordinate a meeting between the Tour and the Saudi PIF. In a matter of weeks — and following numerous international meetings in San Francisco, Milan and London — a "Framework Agreement" was signed by both sides and made public on June 6, 2023. It was a deal to reach a definitive deal, with a roughly 7-month deadline. Monahan and Al-Rumayyan broke the news to the world in a joint interview on CNBC's morning show, Squawk Box, before Mohanan flew to Toronto to face the Tour membership, which was blindsided .

That evening, Monahan held a virtual press conference with golf media, uttering a phrase the Tour would soon regret. It was particularly attractive, Monahan said, "to take a competitor off the board, to have them exist as a partner, not an owner."

All manner of ideas were bandied about during those tense and secret few weeks leading up to the agreement, like the fanciful thought of Al-Rumayyan earning membership at Augusta National, or Tiger Woods and Rory McIlroy owning LIV teams. But ultimately, the peace deal was about two things: 1) Ceasing legal action against each other; and 2) Trying to reach a place of unity that would allow the PGA Tour to receive Saudi investment, where players who left could return and where LIV could find sturdy footing in the global golf calendar.

When the dust settled, the eight months following the signed Framework Agreement will likely serve as the most important era in the league's existence. For starters, the United States government perked up, grilling representatives from the Tour in Washington D.C. about the anti-competitive nature of such a merger. Monahan took a five-week medical leave , returning with a promise that progress was "ongoing." Every few weeks, staffers from each tour provided similarly cagey updates about a definitive deal that was nowhere near definitive. In late November, 2023, the PGA Tour — famously a 501(c)(6) non-profit — filed initial paperwork for PGA Tour Enterprises, a new for-profit arm of its business. Right around that time, Rahm became the newest major LIV signing, agreeing to a deal worth a reported $300 to $400 million. And then, two months later, the PGA Tour announced a landmark investment from Strategic Sports Group, headed by John Henry's Fenway Sports Group. SSG would be investing $1.5 billion into the Tour, marking a valuation of roughly $12.9 billion .

Enterprises was formed for a number of reasons — and has delivered a number of important results, like housing the player equity grants Tour members have since received — but one of them was to create an investment opportunity for the Saudi PIF, which the announcement of Enterprises even acknowledged. Negotiations crawled slowly — Tiger Woods hosted Al-Rumayyan and the Tour's player directors in the Bahamas in March 2024 — but produced no results. Discussions between the two parties continued all the way to the White House in February 2025 , where new President Donald Trump hosted Woods, Al-Rumayyan, Monahan and Adam Scott. While the meeting was publicly deemed "constructive," it was the final time the sides would meet.

The ensuing 12 months saw each side go about their business on their own, with little discussion of reunification. The PGA Tour hired Brian Rolapp as its new CEO, who instituted an aggressive plan to recreate its competitive structure based on fewer events an a greater promotion and relegation system. As Rory McIlroy said just this week in Abu Dhabi, "There's never been a better time to be a professional golfer. You know, talk to Jack Nicklaus or any of these older guys, they would have loved LIV to come around in their day, they would have made more money, and we are all making more money because of it."

But McIlroy, who never feared speaking out on the topic, continued with an ominous hindsight that is growing in popularity these days: "But I do think there has to be a bit of a reset. I've talked about this it. They created a false economy within men's professional golf, and I think that there is going to be a bit of a reset here, just for things to be a little bit more sustainable."

LIV spent its final years finding sporadic success internationally, particularly in Australia and South Africa, golf markets the PGA Tour has not visited for years. But a few key factors mattered far more that their inroads abroad: how many events could it host in the United States, and how many people would tune in for them?

The league had settled into a yearly cadence where most of its early events took place all over the world, with its summer events in America. And despite setting domestic attendance records in August 2025, between stops in Chicago and Indianapolis, hosting events in far-reaching corners of the world caused issues for television audiences that were already paltry. The time zone differential between, say, Saudi Arabia for the league's season-opener, and the American East Coast, required tee times be scheduled late to catch some of the American TV audience … or ignoring that audience altogether.

For any number of reasons — like the decades-old viewing habits pushing golf fans to CBS and NBC, not LIV's home of FOX Sports — golf viewers never tuned in to LIV competition like they have for other pro events. The broadcast was decidedly different and flamboyant, but even its best events were out-rated by the PGA Tour by a scale of 10 to 11x, GOLF.com's James Colgan reported . Considering that a dominant majority of the PGA Tour's core revenues are tied up in television rights — similar to other pro sports leagues — it was a massive failure that only 5% of LIV's revenue came from TV rights. It is virtually impossible for a league to operate on its own if its IP wasn't being widely viewed enough for a major TV network to pay serious money for it.

Despite that, LIV continued to spend lavishly. From its very first event, no cost was spared in building its futuristic fan villages, locking in host courses and, most importantly, collecting talent. In March, LIV flew internationally revered DJ Calvin Harris' to Africa for his first ever performance on the continent — a multi-million-dollar expense for roughly 70 minutes of runtime. But LIV's promise of a sporto-cultural festival experience — one of the few unique things it brought to the golf world — became untenable when Saudi Arabia stopped paying for it. After the PIF pulled funding, LIV hosted just three concerts across seven tournaments, ultimately obfuscating how it canceled concerts in Indianapolis. If anything has been learned, it's that creating mega-wattage events with massive musical acts and building out a different version of what golf tournaments could look like is not cheap. And pro golf may not be big enough to sustain those costs, no matter what league is hosting the events. According to business filings in the United Kingdom, LIV's international events alone incurred losses north of $1 billion over the last four years — losses BC Partners was once interested in, just not interested in enough.

But therein lies the irony to the rise and fall of a rival golf league: it was never making significant money, and yet, it was always flush with Saudi cash, receiving more than $1.3 billion in capital injections in the 15 months before the PIF began turning off the faucet. What was once a firehose splashing the entire industry has been reduced to a slow, court-monitored drip.

articles.title: Cal’s Ron Rivera sends harsh reality check to coach, appears to put job on notice
articles.summary: The Cal Berkeley football team has disappointed this season, and first-year head coach Tosh Lupoi already appears to be on the hot seat. Former NFL head coac...
articles.body:
The Cal Berkeley football team has disappointed this season, and first-year head coach Tosh Lupoi already appears to be on the hot seat.

Former NFL head coach turned Cal Athletic Director and GM Ron Rivera made this clear with comments during KNBR's "Murph & Markus" morning show on Thursday morning.

"Tosh came in as a first-time head coach. He did bring a couple of inexperienced coordinators with him. Things didn't work out the way we needed them to work out on offense," Rivera said.

Lupoi, who played college football at Cal, spent time as an assistant coach at Alabama and as Oregon's defensive coordinator before the Golden Bears hired him.

"He has bumped his head a lot. We have talked a lot, tried to give him a lot of advice, point him in the right direction. Some of it, he's been very receptive, and other portions of it, he hasn't. And it's those things that sometimes you've gotta learn for yourself before you think, ' Oh wow, this is it,'" Rivera continued.

"But I'd like to continue to stress that this is a guy that's learning, growing."

Then came what sounded like a warning shot.

"But now it's time… We have to show that we are growing, there has been some growth and development of our players, our team, and the culture is getting stronger. Those are all things that you have to have going forward."

River added, "We've got to get this foundation put down, we've got to show that we have solid roots in the ground, we are ready to go forward… We're doing the things that we need to do. We're putting the players in position, so let's roll.' And that's what we have to do."

It sounds like Cal's finish to the season will determine whether Lupoi continues as their head coach.

articles.title: Joe Gibbs Racing Wants Spire Bound by an Injunction That Covers Only Gabehart. The Judge Hasn’t Ruled, and Trial Starts Feb. 1
articles.summary: Joe Gibbs Racing wants a judge to hold Chris Gabehart in contempt and bind Spire Motorsports to an injunction that so far covers only him. U.S. District Judg...
articles.body:
Joe Gibbs Racing wants a judge to hold Chris Gabehart in contempt and bind Spire Motorsports to an injunction that so far covers only him. U.S. District Judge Susan Rodriguez heard arguments in mid-October and, according to RACER, did not rule from the bench. NASCAR's championship race is Nov. 8 at Homestead-Miami. This fight has until at least Feb. 1, when trial starts.

In April, Rodriguez granted a preliminary injunction against Gabehart, according to RACER. It bars him from keeping, using, copying or disclosing JGR's confidential information, and from working in the same role at Spire. She did not order him to leave Spire, and he may attend Cup and O'Reilly Series races and perform services he did not perform at JGR in the year before his termination. She denied an injunction against Spire itself because JGR had not yet shown Spire received, accessed or used the information. She also found an 18-month non-compete enforceable, which bars him from serving as competition director. Spire hired him as chief motorsports officer.

RACER reported that Gibbs asked the judge to extend the injunction to Spire, bar Spire from running its current underbody and gearbox cooling approaches until the case is resolved, find Gabehart in contempt, and keep him on administrative leave for the duration of the case. The hearing only addressed whether a contempt hearing is needed.

Gibbs argued that Gabehart kept doing the work of a competition director after the orders took effect, including attending at least 12 Cup competition meetings this year. RACER reported that Spire crew chief Travis Peterson testified Gabehart gave tire pressure numbers at Circuit of the Americas that matched JGR's, and that Peterson "probably" received JGR information verbally from him. Gibbs also pointed to a spreadsheet Gabehart made at Spire, called "CG Master," which it says resembles JGR's "CC Audit."

Spire's lawyers argued the injunction covers only Gabehart, not the team, and that the practices Gibbs describes are common shop talk. They said the improvement came from more spending and driver Daniel Suarez, and pointed to a 50 percent drop in DNFs. They also said Goodyear's recommended tire pressures are available to every team. Spire does not dispute that Gabehart attended meetings or made comments, RACER reported, but says there is no evidence Gibbs documents were transferred to Spire personnel. Gabehart's lawyer called the evidence about his contributions "hazy." Spire has since placed him on administrative leave, and he no longer attends meetings or races, according to the filings RACER described.

Rodriguez said Gabehart's conduct "might have been a little sloppy" and that he should have had better legal guidance, RACER reported. She also said trade secrets can be held in memory and misappropriated, noted there is no evidence the information appeared in Spire's competition materials, and questioned how an order could apply when the parties do not agree on what counts as a trade secret.

A ruling will come at a later date, RACER reported. The trial is scheduled to begin Feb. 1.

Spire says tire pressures come from Goodyear and every team has them. Gibbs says Spire crew chief Travis Peterson testified that Gabehart's numbers matched its own. If a number can come from either place, what exactly is the secret?

articles.title: First-timer Jaypal Malviya earns LA28 quota in 10m air pistol
articles.summary: PUNE: On a day when all eyes on Manu Bhaker to win a medal and a quota place, Jaypal Malviya came unannounced to do the honours at the ISSF World
articles.body: PUNE: On a day when all eyes on Manu Bhaker to win a medal and a quota place, Jaypal Malviya came unannounced to do the honours at the ISSF World Championships in Doha on Thursday.Madhya Pradesh’s Malviya, who was participating in his first international competition in the medals category, won silver in men’s 10m air pistol event and also booked India's first berth for the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics.Malviya, 31, scored 242.2 in the final, while China’s Hu Kai shot 243.9 to win gold. Czech Republic’s Jindrich Dubovy took bronze and the third quota place on offer with a score of 220.9.Malviya had entered the final after shooting 585 in the qualification round.Earlier, Manu Bhaker missed on winning a medal and a quota place after finishing fifth in women’s 10m air pistol event. Manu scored 179.9 in the final and a fourth-place finish would have secured at least a quota as there were two Chinese in the top-four and only one athlete from one country gets the quota from one match.Another Indian, Suruchi Singh, met a similar fate as she finished behind Manu with a score of 158.3. Manu had shot 583, while Suruchi had scored 580 to enter the final.In the men’s final, Malviya. the son of a farmer from MP’s Chhindwara district, got off to a modest start with lower 10s and some 9s in between till his first 12 shots. Though he maintained his ranking in the top-5, he changed gears after the 12 shots with 10.6, 10.2, 10.7 and 10.8 to climb up to second position in the 8-shooter final.In the last four rounds, where bronze and gold were decided, Malviya shot two 9.7s and a 10.7 to stay in the hunt, but Kai's 10.6, 10.7 and a 10.5 in the last three shots gave no chance to the Indian for gold.The final had three Chinese shooters, including Paris Games champion Yu Xie and Hu Kai, who had won all the gold medals in the four World Cups last year. The finalists also had Paris Games bronze medallist Paolo Monna of Italy, however, he crashed out of the final at fifth position, while Xie got eliminated at seventh position.“He was playing only in his first international match, that too at the World Championships. He shot really well despite being shaky in the beginning. articles.title: Lo invisible del deporte: "A veces falta el aire y no sabes lo que pasa"
articles.standfirst: La atleta Blanca Hervás, el peleador de UFC Joel Álvarez y el culturista Kim Ángel cruzan sus experiencias con MARCA y debaten sobre la cara B de su profesión por el documental AMIX además de mostrar sus claves de entrenamiento, descanso y nutrición
articles.summary: La atleta María Hervás, el peleador de UFC Joel Álvarez y el culturista Kim Ángel cruzan sus experiencias con MARCA y debaten sobre la cara B de su profesión por el documental AMIX
articles.body: La primera vez que la hija mayor de Joel Álvarez dijo "papá", él estaba en Abu Dabi. Se enteró por un vídeo. "Yo no lloro, soy de hielo, pero se me cayó una lágrima", cuenta el peleador de la UFC. Cuando a Kim Ángel le preguntan qué le ha dolido perderse por el culturismo, piensa en las llamadas que deja de hacer al acercarse un campeonato y en sus abuelos. Blanca Hervás se acuerda del esquí; llevaba cuatro años sin ponerse unos esquís cuando se preguntó cuántos más pasarían. Las tres respuestas nacen del debate planteado a los tres por MARCA. Los protagonistas de 'Lo invisible', la serie documental de AMIX que ya se puede ver en Prime Video, miden el precio de sus carreras en cosas que cualquiera reconoce. Un vídeo que llega desde casa. Una comida familiar a la que no se va. Algo que hacías cada invierno y un día descubres que llevas años sin hacer. Para Joel, el momento más duro de una pelea llega antes de subirse a la jaula. Está en el corte de peso, cuando el cuerpo empieza a dar señales de alarma y todavía queda la báscula. "Es una parte muy peligrosa. De hecho, para mí es la más peligrosa, mucho más que pelear". En el gimnasio pelea a diario. El corte se concentra en los días previos a competir. Kim reconoce esa espera. En algún campeonato le ha tocado meterse sólo en la sauna y preguntarse si sabría reconocer el límite. "Aunque sean riesgos calculados, el riesgo es alto". Lo difícil, dice, "es tener paciencia justo cuando más ganas tienes de dar el peso y salir de ahí". Blanca sitúa el límite en otro sitio. "Para mí, cuando dejas de disfrutar". A la atleta le cuesta más aceptar un día de descanso que afrontar un entrenamiento duro. "Se sufre muchísimo, pero es que lo buscas y lo quieres otra vez", dice del 400. Por eso confía en su entrenador. "Sabe perfectamente distinguir cuándo estoy cansada, cuándo tengo que parar, cuándo hay que empujar". A Joel le basta con mostrar algún dolor para que su equipo se ponga en alerta. Lo cuenta con humor, como si a los demás les sorprendiera descubrir que a Superman también le duele algo. En casa siente que le toca mantener la cabeza fría cuando llegan los golpes de la vida. Kim piensa en quienes siguen su carrera. "Si ven que flaqueamos, que dudamos de nosotros, ¿qué vamos a inspirarles?". Reconoce que enseñar esa parte era uno de los retos del documental. En un deporte que persigue la perfección física, cuesta hablar de los momentos en los que dejas de creer en ti. Blanca lo vive de otra manera. "Cuando he tenido momentos duros lo he exteriorizado, lo he aceptado y no me he sentido peor por ello". Recuerda una tarde en Miami. Le encantaba vivir allí y disfrutaba entrenando, aunque en competición las cosas no salían. Aquella mañana, tanto ella como su entrenadora habían acabado descontentas con la sesión. Horas después, al salir de la ducha, rompió a llorar. "Me faltaba el aire y no sabía qué me pasaba". Esa misma tarde cogió el coche y fue a hablar con su entrenadora, quien le había dado la oportunidad de irse a Estados Unidos. "Ella apostó por mí y confió en mí casi más que yo". Podía aceptar una crítica cuando se sentaban a hablar con calma. Le hacía daño cuando llegaba desde la frustración de un mal entrenamiento. Meses después regresó a España. Joel vuelve al vídeo de su hija cuando habla de cuánto está dispuesto a sacrificar. Le hizo pensar en todo lo que pasa en casa mientras él viaja, compite o se prepara para una pelea. Y en cuántos momentos como aquel está dispuesto a perderse. Kim conoce ese descuido. En plena preparación pasa tanto tiempo pendiente de sí mismo que deja de llamar, de preguntar y de acudir a reuniones familiares. Después del campeonato recupera la calma y se arrepiente. Se propone corregirlo. Cuando llega la siguiente gran cita, vuelve a costarle. Sus abuelos son quienes le hacen pensar en el tiempo que pasa mientras él prepara una competición. Blanca resume en dos palabras lo que le gustaría devolver a los suyos. "Tiempo, atención". Su familia la ha apoyado en cada decisión y sus amigas han estado cerca en los momentos difíciles. Le gustaría compartir un viaje con ellas o algo más que "una comida un domingo y ya está". Cuando recuerda los Juegos, la imagen que elige para explicar qué significa triunfar es la de tener a su gente cerca y verla feliz. Joel ha visto a gente cercana llorar por una derrota que él ya había asumido. Kim reconoce esa sensación. Está habituado a que un campeonato salga mejor o peor. Lo que le cuesta es ver que a alguien de su entorno le ha afectado más que a él y pensar que le ha decepcionado. Cuando hace balance, piensa en todo lo que hizo hasta llegar allí. Kim quiere que 'Lo invisible' ayude a cambiar la imagen del culturismo. Sabe que el físico es lo primero que se ve y quiere que se entienda la complejidad del trabajo que lo precede. Joel pide que se mire más allá del peleador, hacia quien tiene una familia y una vida cuando se apagan los focos. Blanca lo resume así. "Cada persona tiene una historia, cada persona es un mundo".

articles.title: OTD (06/11/24): Le Bris’ Gamble Leads To Frustration Against Preston
articles.summary: Régis Le Bris faced questions but another clean sheet ensured the Black Cats remained top of the Championship.
articles.body:
On paper, a goalless draw away to Preston North End on a midweek evening hardly represented a disastrous result for a Sunderland side that had made such an impressive start to the 2024/2025 campaign.

However, there was a growing sense of frustration among supporters following a below-par performance at Deepdale, with head coach Régis Le Bris coming under some scrutiny for a team selection that ultimately failed to deliver the desired results.

Much of the criticism centred on the Frenchman's decision to leave out two of Sunderland's standout performers of the season — Patrick Roberts and Romaine Mundle — in favour of Tommy Watson and Aaron Connolly, both of whom were handed their first league starts for the club.

It was a bold call from Le Bris, particularly given the attacking threat Roberts and Mundle had provided during Sunderland's impressive opening months of the campaign. Unfortunately for the head coach, his gamble failed to pay off as the Black Cats struggled to find any real rhythm or fluency in the final third.

Neither Watson nor Connolly managed to make a significant impression, although the latter came closest to breaking the deadlock when he was denied his first Sunderland goal by a fine close-range save from Freddie Woodman following some excellent work by Trai Hume — yet that this represented arguably Sunderland's best opportunity of the evening spoke volumes about the nature of the contest.

It was a largely forgettable affair in which clear-cut chances were at a premium, with Sunderland's defensive unit once again doing much of the heavy lifting to ensure that the visitors returned to Wearside with something to show for their efforts.

Unsurprisingly, Le Bris faced questions afterwards about whether his decision to make such significant changes had hindered his side's chances of securing all three points.

However, the Frenchman remained steadfast in his belief that managing the demands of a gruelling Championship campaign required more than simply relying on the same starting eleven every week.

articles.title: Russell reveals emotional toll of nightmare season: 'I feel a bit exhausted'
articles.summary: George Russell has admitted that he feels mentally exhausted after repeatedly dealing with setbacks throughout the 2026 season, with the Mercedes driver reve...
articles.body:
George Russell has admitted that he feels mentally exhausted after repeatedly dealing with setbacks throughout the 2026 season, with the Mercedes driver revealing how difficult it has become to recover from disappointment after disappointment.

The Briton arrived at the Brazilian Grand Prix following another frustrating weekend in Mexico, where he started second on the grid and believed he had a genuine opportunity to fight for victory. However, technical problems once again disrupted his race , leaving him unable to capitalise on his promising starting position.

The latest setback added to a growing list of difficulties for Russell, who has struggled to turn Mercedes' competitive pace into consistent results this season. To make matters worse, he watched teammate Kimi Antonelli secure the title in Mexico, while Russell's own title ambitions came to an end. His frustration was evident after the race, as he did not attend the post-race media interviews.

Russell opens up about mental toll of difficult Mercedes season

Speaking ahead of the Brazilian Grand Prix, Russell explained that the repeated setbacks have taken a significant emotional toll, particularly as he has continually tried to recover and approach each race with renewed optimism.

"I probably just feel a bit exhausted this season of constantly picking myself back up. When you get kicked to the ground, you pick yourself back up, and then you kick down again, you pick yourself back up. And I was hoping to do that maybe twice in the season, not every other weekend, really.

"When you get to a point of this season, you're away from home for three weeks in a row and you have another race like what happened in Mexico where a chance of victory, a chance of the podium just disappears totally outside of your control is tough to deal with. It's very tough to deal with."

Despite returning to the circuit where he celebrated his maiden Formula 1 victory, Russell admitted that he is approaching the Brazilian weekend without particularly high expectations.

"Brazil is a place that I love. I've got great memories of. Do I come in with high expectations? Honestly, no, to be honest. But looking forward to next year for sure, and we'll just continue to work on the things that I can control and pray the things outside of my control sort themselves up."

Russell also stressed that his confidence in his own abilities remains intact, despite the difficulties he has experienced throughout the campaign: "I don't think there's a single athlete in the world or business person or even just individual in life that goes through every single year having great years. All of us in this room have good days. We have bad days. We have good years. We have bad years for different reasons.

"The goats in sports have years that have been tough for them. We were talking about Lewis before. He's had so many successful years, but he's also had tough years, and it's the way you sort of bounce back from those years to continue having the belief and courage to return to those positive ways and that mental resilience.

"And I think that for me is what I have, what this year has taught me. I still believe in myself and believe next year, we fight again."

articles.title: Sunderland’s Woes Can’t Solely Be Pinned On Régis Le Bris
articles.summary: The beleaguered Sunderland gaffer deserves better than what he’s currently enduring, writes Tom Albrighton.
articles.body:
He's chased a new style. It isn't working and now he's too stubborn to go back on it.

His stubborness is killing him. Too many players beyond reproach, the same worn out tactics, the same predictable outcomes — and the same style of play not suiting the players we have.

He's ran out of ideas because he hasn't got the courage to drop the offenders and to take the risks he needs to take. As a result, the squad has lost its identity because the guiding light at the top doesn't know where he wants to be — or he does know and he doesn't know how to get there.

He has his failings — his like-for-like subs, the way we start games, the general and complete lack or urgency or vertical play, and what kills him more is that we see flashes of the Sunderland that endeared themselves to the fans last season — but he refuses to accept this is the way.

He deserved more than a summer of speculation about his future which was a thinly-veiled temperature test of the fans' openness to a new gaffer, and he deserved so much more than the owner not coming out publicly to rubbish them.

He deserved much better than his captain publicly flirting with the idea of returning to his lavish London lifestyle on a six-figure weekly salary…only to bottle it for the fear of backlash and to turn up this season half-arsing it because the mind and the body are in two different places.

He deserves more than players playing like idiots because it's easier to throw everything into it when things are going well — and you're the one taking the plaudits than it is to throw yourself out there for the man who guided you to them.

He deserved more than a joke of a summer where the sporting director spent more time flirting with the idea of signing players than actually doing so, not building the depth we desperately needed and not having the courage to be bold in the market like the season before, but instead leaning heavily on the phone book and vibes.

He deserves more than having Michael Proctor as an assistant and a set piece coach that thinks having eleven men defending a corner is a legitimate tactic.

He deserves so much more than what he's got from the people around him and he can't move without failing because the board spent most of the summer sat on their sun loungers, chuffing cigars and musing about how great they all are.

Five like-for-like subs when the system hasn't worked for weeks? Bollocks. Not knowing his best eleven? Bollocks. The way we set up? Bollocks. And there's loads more on him too.

Ultimately, he's gone. It's just a matter of time but if there aren't rakes of others culpable for this, I'll be damned.

The New York Yankees want to keep closer David Bednar and believe they have all the advantages to re-sign him. MLB fans are expecting a noteworthy offseason, and the Yankees have already made headlines with a couple of important decisions. Bednar received his qualifying offer to show the Yankees hope to retain his services. Jazz Chisholm did not receive a similar offer and is expected to leave the team in free agency.

The Athletic's Brendan Kuty revealed that the Yankees believe their pitching coaches are a huge benefit to keep Bednar:

"Last offseason, the New York Yankees pitching department mapped out a slight grip change for closer David Bednar's splitter. It was something the right-hander worked on throughout the winter, and when both sides agreed he should throw it more often, the pitch became the centerpiece of his arsenal. The Yankees may feel exceptionally comfortable in bringing back Bednar is the connection he made with their pitching coaches and how he showed an impressive ability to learn, helping lead to his dominant 2026."

November 17 is the deadline for Bednar to make a final decision on whether he's accepting the Yankees' qualifying offer or not. New York has a tremendous pitching staff anchored by Cy Young favorite Cam Schlittler and just needs a reliable bullpen to round out the pitching.

Re-signing Judge and going above their usual salary desires also proved that the right talents could get the big bucks from the Yankees . Bednar is clearly below both names, but reliable relievers are more valuable than ever with offense down and starting pitchers having strict pitch counts.

The Yankees will hope to get more out of homegrown players like Spencer Jones and Anthony Volpe . Smart money is on New York keeping Bednar to anchor their bullpen to continue having a top pitching roster. However, more offense will be needed for the Yankees to contend for the World Series.

articles.title: New Covenant claims first state volleyball crown: 'We wanted to dominate'
articles.summary: New Covenant volleyball swept Woodland to secure the school's first-ever state championship. How the team made their dreams a reality.
articles.body:
When New Covenant started summer workouts, the Warriors had one single goal. Every day, New Covenant spoke about winning the Class 2 State Championship.

Players thought about hoisting the title during practice, at school and at home. They finally realized their dreams on Thursday, Nov. 5.

New Covenant swept Woodland 3-0 (25-18, 25-22, 25-17) for the school's first state title.

"This is just so exciting to come and actually win a state championship," outside hitter Lexi Burks said. "To say you are going to do it is one thing, but to actually do it is incredible."

New Covenant were the aggressors throughout the title match. Not only did they want to win, but the Warriors also wanted to sweep.

See the photos from New Covenant volleyball's state title vs Woodland

Sweeping teams has been New Covenant's bread and butter this season. The Warriors have won 24 of their 37 matches in three-set sweeps. The team's offense has pummeled the opposition, while great defense has kept rallies alive. Woodland were the latest to feel the Warriors' wrath.

"We came in and we wanted to dominate this game and take state," Burks said. "I think that's really what helped us pull out this win."

The first set featured just two lead changes as New Covenant kept its foot on the gas pedal. Woodland had its best chance in set two. The Cardinals led 20-19, but New Covenant closed on a 6-2 run. The third set showcased even more dominance. The Warriors never trailed and led by as many as 10 points.

Burks was outstanding for New Covenant. She led the team with 16 kills and 13 digs. The senior was insanely efficient with a hitting percentage of .519. Altogether, the Warriors hit .303 and earned eight aces.

New Covenant Academy volleyball: Lexi Burks helps Warriors chase state title

Along with Burks, five other New Covenant players tallied a kill. One of the team's most impactful players was Kiera Edwards. Off the bench, Edwards recorded 12 kills, the second-most on the team.

Edwards didn't have just one strong game. She was the difference in the semifinals, too. The sophomore led the team with 15 kills in New Covenant's five-set thriller versus Mid-Buchanan on Wednesday, Nov. 4.

"She was on fire," Burks said about Edwards. "She was doing amazing. For her to be a sophomore and to be swinging like the way that she was, she did amazing tonight."

The team's offensive efficiency came directly from precise passing. Addy Mourey and Lillie Chapey delivered perfect pass after perfect pass. Chapey ended with 18 assists, while Mourey finished with 17.

Libero Jenna Jackson, middle hitter Tina Voznyarska, defensive specialist Myah Vinson and Burks made good on their promise to deliver New Covenant a state title. This senior class will always be remembered for delivering the program its first championship.

The future is quite bright for the Warriors, though. Six players that featured in the state championship will return for head coach Chenille Gaumer.

"We have a bright future and in the last few years, it's been growing," Burks said. "I think New Covenant will continue to make a name for itself."

articles.title: Not the prettiest match, but Wisconsin volleyball outlasts Michigan State
articles.summary: Wisconsin coach Kelly Sheffield was quick to say it "wasn't the prettiest match," but the Badgers came away with a four-set win over Michigan State.
articles.body:
MADISON – The Wisconsin volleyball team might not have picked up many style points against Michigan State , finishing with fewer kills, more attack errors and a worse hitting percentage.

But the seventh-ranked Badgers earned enough actual points to outlast the Spartans in four sets, 24-26, 25-21, 27-25, 25-20, on Nov. 5 at the UW Field House for their 91st consecutive win against an unranked opponent.

Wisconsin 's .199 hitting percentage was its lowest in a win in 2026. (The Badgers previously were 0-5 when hitting below .200.)

"It wasn't the prettiest match out there," Wisconsin coach Kelly Sheffield said. "But it was two teams that were working. … We found a way."

Here are three takeaways from the Badgers' win over the Spartans:

Best photos from Wisconsin volleyball's matches vs Washington, Michigan

Wisconsin's run late in third set serves as turning point

Michigan State appeared to be one point away from taking a 2-1 set lead, facing set point with a 24-22 lead. (The Spartans had a 23-19 lead before that as well.)

But then the Badgers went on a spirited 5-1 run to take the set, 27-22.

Jaela Auguste and Halle Thompson's kills tied it at 24-24 after two rallies with no margin for error.

Then after a Michigan State block, Wisconsin scored the next three points on a Decelise Champion kill, Michigan State attack error and Charlie Fuerbringer ace to finish off the pivotal third set.

"You've got to play clean," Sheffield said. "You've got to read the game. … Made a couple big-time plays there and just stayed within ourselves. And we've got that ability to do that, and the idea is to try to tap into that more and more frequently."

The comeback was a sharp contrast from earlier in the Michigan State match, when the Badgers gave up three consecutive points to go from a UW set point to a Michigan State set victory.

It also served as a reversal of fortunes from the Badgers' loss to then-No. 21 Washington on Oct. 23. That was when the Badgers blew 23-19 and 24-22 leads in the second set of an eventual five-set loss.

The successful third set was a turning point in the match. After 13 ties and four lead changes in the third set, UW never trailed after 5-4 in the fourth set and would have won even more comfortably without Michigan State's late 5-0 run.

"Sometimes when things aren't going well, it tests you mentally and emotionally, and it tests your resolve to stay together," Sheffield said. "And I thought we did a really good job – better than maybe what we've done in some other matches when it hasn't come easy."

Jaela Auguste responds in big way after getting benched at UCLA

After getting held out of the UCLA match, Wisconsin middle blocker Jaela Auguste had a starring role in the Badgers' win over the Spartans.

The 2025 third-team All-American recorded 14 kills with only one attack error, resulting in a .542 hitting percentage. The 14 kills were the second-most for Auguste in a match this season, trailing only her 20-kill performance against Iowa.

Sheffield also gave his setter Fuerbringer credit after Auguste's efficient performance.

"Charlie was really delivering some really nice balls," Sheffield said. "There was a few of those that you really kind of see her talent of, some situations, hitting Jaela in stride. … The connection was on, and she can be a handful for opponents when that connection is strong."

It was a sound performance from the middle blocker position as a whole.

Freshman (and fellow starter) Lynney Tarnow had eight kills and a team-high six blocks. Two attack errors brought her hitting percentage down to .375, and Sheffield saw some missed opportunities early on that she overcame.

"It was a slow start for her early," Sheffield said. "I thought she missed on some great overpass opportunities that I'm sure will keep her awake a little bit tonight. … She flushes things about as well as any young player I've ever coached, and her numbers end up being pretty good."

Grace Egan sees bigger role as Michigan State's serve provides challenge

Michigan State's two aces will hardly stand out on the box score after a four-set match.

But the Badgers quietly felt the serving pressure.

"If you stood behind the end line, you just see what some of those serves were doing and their ability to get into different spaces," Sheffield said. "You have to flush what happened previously and just be tough."

While outside hitter Eva Travis started the first set, the Spartans' serving pressure affected how the Badgers used the UC-Santa Barbara transfer for the rest of the match. She did not play in the second and fourth sets and subbed in during the third set.

Kristen Simon started the second, third and fourth sets as a defensive specialist in Travis' place.

"Can you handle the ball against an elite serving team?" Sheffield said. "We were spending quite a bit of time in kind of medium-pass situations or out of system. And can you take good swings and score? Eva was a little error-prone in both of those areas."

Travis' reduced role also led to more pronounced roles for Grace Egan and Thompson – two players Sheffield said he thought were "ready for the moment and ready to be in there."

Thompson had two kills and two attack errors, finishing with a .000 hitting percentage. Egan had two attack errors and no kills, hitting minus-.400. But their passing was critical, and playing in the front row was another sign of progress for Egan after her significant back injury and lengthy recovery.

"Grace gave us a lift certainly from a passing perspective," Sheffield said. "She's still working on that jump, still not contacting that ball where she was at the height. And that's still to be kind of a work in progress."

Freshman (and fellow starter) Lynney Tarnow had eight kills and a team-high six blocks. Two attack errors brought her hitting percentage down to .375, and Sheffield saw some missed opportunities early on that she overcame.

"It was a slow start for her early," Sheffield said. "I thought she missed on some great overpass opportunities that I'm sure will keep her awake a little bit tonight. … She flushes things about as well as any young player I've ever coached, and her numbers end up being pretty good."

Grace Egan sees bigger role as Michigan State's serve provides challenge

Michigan State's two aces will hardly stand out on the box score after a four-set match.

But the Badgers quietly felt the serving pressure.

"If you stood behind the end line, you just see what some of those serves were doing and their ability to get into different spaces," Sheffield said. "You have to flush what happened previously and just be tough."

While outside hitter Eva Travis started the first set, the Spartans' serving pressure affected how the Badgers used the UC-Santa Barbara transfer for the rest of the match. She did not play in the second and fourth sets and subbed in during the third set.

Kristen Simon started the second, third and fourth sets as a defensive specialist in Travis' place.

"Can you handle the ball against an elite serving team?" Sheffield said. "We were spending quite a bit of time in kind of medium-pass situations or out of system. And can you take good swings and score? Eva was a little error-prone in both of those areas."

Travis' reduced role also led to more pronounced roles for Grace Egan and Thompson – two players Sheffield said he thought were "ready for the moment and ready to be in there."

Thompson had two kills and two attack errors, finishing with a .000 hitting percentage. Egan had two attack errors and no kills, hitting minus-.400. But their passing was critical, and playing in the front row was another sign of progress for Egan after her significant back injury and lengthy recovery.

"Grace gave us a lift certainly from a passing perspective," Sheffield said. "She's still working on that jump, still not contacting that ball where she was at the height. And that's still to be kind of a work in progress."

articles.title: Michigan vs. Michigan State Score Prediction: Will the Wolverines Roll Under the Lights in Ann Arbor?
articles.summary: Michigan enters its rivalry showdown with Michigan State as a 13.5-point favorite, but can the Wolverines' struggling offense do enough to complement an elit...
articles.body:
Michigan and Michigan State will renew their bitter rivalry Saturday night in Ann Arbor, with kickoff scheduled for 7:30 p.m. The Wolverines enter as 13.5-point favorites, and on paper, they should have a significant advantage over the Spartans.

Michigan has struggled offensively throughout the season, but its defense remains one of the nation's best. Against a Michigan State team struggling on both sides of the ball, the Wolverines have an opportunity to put together one of their most complete performances of the season.

Michigan's offense has been anything but explosive this season, averaging just 21.25 points and 316.4 yards per game. The Wolverines are producing 138 rushing yards and 178.4 passing yards per contest, numbers that have made sustained offensive success difficult.

However, Michigan State presents an opportunity to get things going.

The Spartans are surrendering 25.75 points and 355.1 total yards per game, including 153.8 yards on the ground. They've also forced just six turnovers in eight games.

Michigan freshman quarterback Tommy Carr showed encouraging signs against Rutgers, and another week of experience should help him continue developing. With Jordan Marshall, Savion Hiter and the rest of Michigan's rushing attack facing a vulnerable defense, the Wolverines should emphasize establishing the ground game early.

Michigan's biggest concern remains finishing drives. The Wolverines have scored touchdowns on just 14 of 24 red-zone opportunities, something that could prevent this game from becoming a blowout.

This is where Michigan has an overwhelming advantage.

The Wolverines rank third nationally in total defense, allowing just 250 yards per game. They're also surrendering only 16.4 points per contest while limiting opponents to 99.4 rushing yards and 150.6 passing yards.

Michigan State's offense, meanwhile, is averaging just 19.9 points and 291.4 yards per game.

The Spartans have struggled to establish consistency on the ground, averaging 110.1 rushing yards per contest, and quarterback Alessio Milivojevic will face a defense capable of creating significant pressure, if he can go. He's currently questionable, so freshman Kayd Coffman is preparing as well.

Michigan has recorded 18 sacks and seven interceptions, while Michigan State enters with a minus-six turnover margin.

If the Jay Hill's unit can eliminate Michigan State's running game and force obvious passing situations, the Spartans could struggle to sustain drives throughout the evening.

Everything about this matchup suggests Michigan should win comfortably. The Wolverines possess a dramatically better defense, have home-field advantage and should benefit from a fired-up crowd under the lights.

Still, Michigan's offensive inconsistencies make covering a 13.5-point spread less automatic than the talent disparity might suggest.

The Wolverines don't necessarily need an explosive performance from Carr to win. They simply need to protect the football, establish the running game and allow their defense to dictate the contest.

Michigan State's offense doesn't appear equipped to consistently move the football against this defense, and that should ultimately be the difference.

The rivalry factor could keep things competitive early, but Michigan should gradually pull away as its defensive superiority takes over.

The Wolverines cover the 13.5-point spread, improve their offensive production and secure a convincing rivalry victory in Ann Arbor. Paul Bunyan will stay at The Big House for another year.

articles.title: Will Mencl rallies Chandler past Hamilton for big football rivalry win
articles.summary: The No. 2 Chandler Wolves defeated No. 3 Hamilton on Thursday, Nov. 5. Both will advance to the Open Division playoffs.
articles.body:
Chandler's football team made a statement before the opening kickoff when the players ran through Hamilton's entry lane formed by band members and cheerleaders.

The most intense Arizona high school football rivalry, known as the Battle For Arizona Avenue, was on at Hamilton High School in Chandler.

It took a 14-0 deficit for quarterback Will Mencl to rally Chandler to a 31-24 6A football victory in the final regular-season game before an overflow crowd at Hamilton on Thursday night, Nov. 5.

No. 2 Chandler (6A AIA/MaxPreps ranking) finished the regular season 9-1. Hamilton (No. 3) finished 8-2.

Mencl threw two touchdown passes and ran for two others in Thursday's win.

Last year, after the Wolves lost to Hamilton in the final regular-season game, Mencl tore apart Hamilton with his legs in a 30-17 Open Division semifinal playoff win, in which he ran for 105 yards and three TDs.

The teams will find out Saturday morning, Nov. 7, where they're seeded in the Open Division state playoffs when the 12-team bracket is released.

Mencl, on a fourth-and-1 play, broke loose up the middle for a 62-yard touchdown that tied the score at 24-24 with 1:59 left in the third quarter.

Then, shaking off an interception, Mencl drove Chandler downfield on a 73-yard scoring drive, completing three straight passes, running for an 11-yard gain, before capping it with a 4-yard touchdown run that gave Chandler its first lead, 31-24, with 6:57 to play, which turned out to be the final score.

"Just telling Coach Wiz (Ty Wisdom) I want the ball in my hands," Mencl said, about preparing for his team's rival.

Jax Sculley, Mencl's counterpart, was having a remarkable game early on. In the opening series, he found Christian Riley deep for a 73-yard gain. Sculley capped that with a 1-yard scoring sneak. Then, after Chandler turned the ball over, Hamilton cashed in with Sculley finding Riley for a 2-yard touchdown play.

Sculley later hit Roman Oliver for a 42-yard scoring play, giving Hamilton a 21-14 lead after Chandler had tied the game Mencl's 4-yard scoring pass to Daniel Martinez.

Wisdom kept dialing up plays for Mencl, and the Oregon commit kept delivering in the clutch.

"There was self-inflicted stuff early," Wisdom said. "But if you were on our sideline, you didn't see a lot of panic. We all know crazy things are going to happen in a rivalry game. But I was proud of our guys. They kept coming back. I thought the defense played a lot better in the second half."

Chandler limited Hamilton to just a field goal in the second half.

Mencl helped the Wolves run off the final 5:33 after Hamilton (8-2) had to punt it away. He was helped out by a 15-yard personal foul after sliding in and getting hit late over the top of his body. He scampered for an 11-yard gain later in the drive, moving the sticks. Hamilton ran out of time outs and, on the last play, Mencl, looking at the clock, ran backwards and purposely took an 18-yard sack.

Chandler didn't have to run another play.

"I told him this last week, 'I want the ball in your hands. If I'm going to go down, I'm going to go down with you.' " Wisdom said of Mencl. "He made a lot of big plays tonight."

"It's not fun being hit late, but it's part of the game," Mencl said. "We respect these guys down the street. They did a really good job game planning for us.

"I was just trying to be that guy. It centered on me a little bit. So I just popped up every time, and kept my head up, knowing we have to go back to work."

Chandler plays with a swagger. It showed before the kickoff, as Hamilton coaches were furious that Chandler players ran down their lane.

Mencl said he didn't realize the team was running through Hamilton's lane before the game.

"I was just running out talking as much as I possibly could," Mencl said. "They have the student section right next to our locker room. So coming out people were throwing stuff at us. We had to represent Chandler. It's a good rivalry game. There's a lot of tradition and legacy. So to come out with this win, it's great to talk about it."
